title: Metric Spaces: Distance as Data
notes: Open by positioning Chapter 1 as the instrument panel for the rest of metric geometry. The audience should hear that a metric is not merely a formula for length. It is the data structure from which topology, limits, compactness, and dimension will be recovered throughout the course.

title: What Does Distance Control?
notes: Use the map to create a promise for the lecture. Each stop answers one question: what are distances allowed to be, how can one set carry different geometries, what does local distance control imply, and how does scale bookkeeping lead to dimension?

title: Metric Axioms as a Distance Table
notes: Treat the finite table as a laboratory version of the definition. Point to the diagonal, symmetry across the diagonal, and one triangle comparison. The goal is not to compute every inequality by hand, but to make the axioms visible enough that later abstract examples feel testable.

title: Infinite Metrics Split Space Into Components
notes: Explain why allowing infinity is not a defect in this chapter. Finite distance defines components, and the metric inside each component behaves normally. The dashed cross-component separations mark that no finite path of distance information connects the two pieces.

title: Semi-Metrics Become Metrics After a Quotient
notes: The quotient slide should slow the room down. A semi-metric can say that two different points are at zero distance. The repair is not to pretend they are distinct, but to identify each zero-distance fiber and measure the resulting classes.

title: Same Set, Different Geometry
notes: Here the main message is that geometry lives in the metric, not only in the underlying set. The log metric compresses far distances, norm balls reveal different notions of unit step, dilation rescales every comparison, and chord versus arc distance changes what shortest means.

title: Finite-Dimensional Norms
notes: Use the nested norm balls to distinguish shape from topology. In finite-dimensional spaces the balls look different, but each norm bounds the others after changing constants. That is the bi-Lipschitz lesson: the topology survives even when the unit geometry changes.

title: Metric Topology Begins With Balls
notes: Turn topology into a concrete observational rule. Around every point, the metric supplies balls, and those balls decide which sets are open. The slide should make students inspect how changing the metric changes the neighborhoods before any theorem is invoked.

title: Lipschitz Maps
notes: Emphasize Lipschitz maps as controlled functions. Continuity only asks that nearby inputs eventually give nearby outputs; Lipschitz control gives a single global rate. The distance-to-a-set example is useful because the slope bound is visible.

title: Completeness
notes: Define completeness as an internal landing guarantee. A Cauchy sequence can behave as though it is converging using only distances among its terms. If the proposed landing point is missing, as in a punctured space, the metric record exposes the gap.

title: Compactness
notes: Compactness should feel finite-resolution rather than mystical. At every epsilon scale, finitely many balls see the whole space, and completeness prevents Cauchy tails from escaping. The circle example gives the audience something to inspect at a fixed resolution.

title: Compact Self-Isometries
notes: Use this proof scaffold as a story about not losing distance data. If a distance-preserving self-map of a compact space missed a point, a positive gap would let us add one more separated point than compactness permits. That is the contradiction.

title: Hausdorff Measure
notes: Hausdorff measure is introduced as paying for a cover. The exponent d changes the price of a small set: small intervals become cheap faster when d is larger. This prepares the critical exponent without requiring a full measure theory detour.

title: Hausdorff Dimension
notes: The Cantor calculation is the memorable endpoint. At d equal to log two over log three, the stage weights stay level; below it they grow, above it they shrink. This is the operational meaning of dimension in this first lecture.

title: What Survives Under Distance Control?
notes: Close by returning to the chapter question: what information is carried by distances alone? The recap should make clear that Chapter 1 already supplies a toolkit: quotienting, examples, topology, Lipschitz control, completeness, compactness, and dimension.
